newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-UK gilts to prosper after elections.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-UK gilts to prosper after elections.

text.p: UK gilts could prosper, at least relative to other bond markets, in 1997 but will probably have to wait until an approaching general election is out of the way to enjoy better times, a Reuters survey shows.

Reuters polled 17 economists based in the U.K. and found that their average predictions for the gilt/Bund spread was 194 basis points by the end of March, little changed at 189 by the end of June but falling to 166 by the end of the year.
Elections are due by May but could come earlier with the Conservative government robbed of its parliamentary majority.
Forecasts ranged across a wide spectrum but only one of the economists expected the spread to be significantly wider by the end of this year than the 185 basis points it stands at now.
For the first quarter, forecasts for the premium at which 10-year British government bonds trade over their German counterparts stretched from 175 to 210 basis points.

Before the 1992 election, the gilt/Bund spread reached a peak of 227 basis points. Then, as now, a Labour government was expected to take power. When the ruling Conservatives were voted back in, gilts rallied.
This time, analysts said there were fewer concerns about a prospective Labour government's economic policies, so the spread would be unlikely to gape as far as it did five years ago.
Opinion polls have consistently put the Labour Party 20 percent or more ahead of the Conservatives.

"Our view is that new Labour will not repeat the policies of the past, which will remove some of the fear factor. But it will take time for them to establish their credentials," said Philip Shaw, group economist at Union Plc.
He forecast a gilt/Bund spread of 200 basis points by the end of March, falling to 150 by the year-end.
Shaw said another factor holding the gilt market back in the near term was that Britain was the only major European economy looking to raise interest rates.
Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke increased base rates by a quarter percentage point to six percent in October and could well repeat the move in the next few weeks.

But in Europe, economies struggling to get into shape for a single European currency have been pushed close, or into, recession, leaving interest rates at historically low levels and showing no signs of heading higher.
Though a Labour government may hold fewer terrors for the gilt market nowadays, the Reuters poll showed investors holding gilts outright will be lucky to make a profit this year.
The consensus forecast put the 10-year gilt yield at 7.77 percent by the end of March. It was trading at 7.63 percent on Friday.

By the end of the year, the average forecast put the benchmark gilt yield at eight percent, presumably dragged lower by bearish bond markets in Germany and the United States, although outperforming as they all head lower.
The survey produced an average forecast of 7.72 percent for the gilt yield by the end of 1998. So, the next two years do not look like they will offer rich pickings.
But in spread terms, next year could also be a positive one for the British debt market. The consensus forecast for the gilt/Bund spread at the end of 1998 was 141 basis points.
But that performance does not mean Britain is likely to sign up for a single European currency in the first wave, scheduled for January 1, 1999.
"We are unlikely to enter a single European single currency in 1999," Shaw said. "If we do, the spread will be in double figures, not three."
